title: ApiResponse and ApiError
idea: ApiResponse and ApiError are two small classes that give every reply one JSON shape, so clients can read successes and failures the same way.

analogy.text: A standard shipping label. Every parcel, whatever is inside, carries sender, address and status in the same slots, so any scanner can read it.
analogy.breaks: Contents differ; only the label's layout is fixed.

points: `success` is computed as `statusCode < 400`; you never set it by hand.
`ApiError` extends `Error`, so `throw new ApiError(404, ...)` works inside any handler.
A handler turns a thrown `ApiError` into JSON; unknown errors become a generic 500.

hero.title: Two shapes, one envelope
hero.verdict: Clients check `success` first, then read `data` or `errors`.

code.caption: Save as `src/utils/api-response.js`. The status is a plain number; `success` follows from it.

walk.text: Extending `Error` makes it throwable, with a stack trace.
`errors` defaults to `[]`, so clients can always loop over it.
Keep the status, the field details and a `false` success flag.
Use a stack passed in, or capture a clean one.

walk.text: A success: wrap the data in `ApiResponse` and set the same HTTP status.
Failures are thrown. `errors` holds per-field details.
A bug throws a plain error, not an `ApiError`.
Four arguments mark an error handler. Anything but an `ApiError` becomes a generic 500.
Build the body by hand: sending `err` itself would drop `message`.
Call each route and print the status and JSON body.
Close the server so the script can exit.

pitfalls: `ApiResponse` does not set the HTTP status. Call `res.status(code)` with the same number.
Do not send the error object itself: `JSON.stringify` drops its `message`. Build the body.
Never put `err.stack` or raw internal messages in a reply; log them on the server.

quiz.why: `ApiError` extends `Error`, so `instanceof` is true. `errors` defaults to an empty array, so its length is 0.

takeaway: One envelope for every reply: `success` first, then `data` or `errors`.
